subject: Next steps: Reserved capacity acceptance criteria and hyperscaler fallback tests

Subject: Intro + reserved capacity questions

Hi Vanessa,

Thanks again for the call earlier — good overview. A couple of follow-ups from our side as we evaluate reserved GPU commitments vs keeping everything on CloudScale:

- Can you send a short acceptance criteria checklist you would run in a live comparison? We want to validate throughput, tail latency during spikes, and graceful fallback to a cloud provider if dedicated pools are saturated.
- We also need a clear list of what Redwood requires to guarantee capacity (commit levels, lead time, pre-warm options) and what your typical overbooking policy looks like.
- Any examples of how you’ve structured canary/fallback routing in production? We care about predictable failover — ability to route to a compatible model with minimal client-side changes.

Attached is a very rough spreadsheet of our expected traffic ranges and peak patterns. Please take a look and propose the right reserve tiers.

Couple of additional asks: pricing for 3/6/12 month reserved tiers, and whether you can offer any onboarding credit for the pilot.

Best,
Priya Shah
Head of ML Engineering, ACME Corp
(attachment: capacity-matrix.xlsx)

From: vanessa_ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Intro + reserved capacity questions

Hi Priya — thanks for the clear list, very helpful. Recap from our side and proposed next steps below.

Quick recap of differentiators relevant to the comparison:
- Predictable throughput: Dedicated pools give a guaranteed baseline of GPU slots with autoscale/burst policies you define.
- Cost controls: Intelligent batching + KV cache reduces per-token compute; we can show measured unit cost over your sample workload.
- Graceful degradation: Automatic model-variant routing + per-request fallback policies so a client-facing endpoint can transparently drop to a quantized or smaller variant if dedicated capacity is unavailable.

Proposed acceptance criteria for the comparative run (we’ll formalize into the PDF test plan):
1) Steady-state throughput: sustain 400 qps with p95 latency <= 220ms and p50 <= 90ms for your file-based workload.
2) Spike behavior: under 3x burst (simulated traffic for 5 minutes), p99 should remain under 950ms and error rate < 1%.
3) Failover correctness: if Dedicated pool intentionally drained, requests should fallback to a compatible hosted variant with <2s end-to-end client-visible failover and no data loss.
4) Cost baseline: measured cost-per-1k-tokens across the run and delta vs CloudScale on same workload.
5) KV cache hit rate target: >30% for repeated-session workloads to prove cost/latency wins.

Requested inputs from ACME to finalize plan:
- Representative prompt set and payload sizes (sample subset is fine)
- Typical session length and concurrency distribution during peak
- Any regulatory constraints for traffic routing (e.g., all inference must stay in us-west-2)

Planned timeline / next steps:
- I’ll attach a short test plan PDF with concrete test cases and measurement harness (attached).
- Proposal: run a 3-day comparative test window week of Nov 9. Redwood will own the Dedicated pool configuration and test runner; ACME + CloudScale to run the same harness against CloudScale endpoints.
- Marissa will own pricing/commit tiers and a draft reserve proposal; Rishi will run the tuning recommendations for batching/quant profiles before the run.

Attachments: redwood-vs-hyperscaler-test-plan.pdf (first draft), capacity-matrix.xlsx (from ACME)

If that works, can you confirm the traffic window and whether Nov 9-11 is acceptable? I’ll schedule a short kickoff.

Thanks,
Vanessa Ortiz
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
(attachment: redwood-vs-hyperscaler-test-plan.pdf)

Subject: Fwd: Intro + reserved capacity questions — internal notes

Looping in quick internal playbook notes for the Nov test window. Forwarding Vanessa's draft plan and adding tactical asks.

Positioning bullets (short):
- Predictability > raw peak: emphasize committed baseline and predictable per-token unit economics for budget owners.
- Failure surface minimized: explain model-variant routing as "transparent fallback" not "manual failover"; demo with a simple API flag.
- Ops overhead low: we manage pre-warm and autoscale; customers manage commit level and policy.

Tactical checklist (owners):
- Marissa: draft 3/6/12 month price matrix and onboarding credit options (due 2026-11-02).
- Rishi: provide quantization + batch configs for ACME sample prompts; run offline sim and share expected p95/p99 deltas (due 2026-11-04).
- Logan: prepare the test harness container and a quick script to seed KV cache for repeated-session tests; verify metrics export to ACME's CloudWatch stack (due 2026-11-06).

Questions to raise with ACME on kickoff:
1) Do they want network-level failover (BGP) or application-level routing (API redirect + client retry)? Our preference: app-level for simpler instrumentation.
2) Will they accept model-variant fallbacks (quantized) for <2s failover window, or require full fidelity always?

I’ll join the kickoff. If anyone sees a risk (especially around regulatory routing or audit logs), flag it now.

-Marissa
Director, Customer Solutions
